title: When Words Are the Math Problem
author: Beanie
summary: This piece, previously published at Freedom in Education, starts from a parent's lament that children who are great at math freeze when problems arrive as word problems. The author argues that parents and teachers often blame math skills while overlooking literacy: students must decode and comprehend the language before they can apply any math. Citing Doug Lemov on dysfluency, she says slow word recognition consumes working memory and crowds out understanding. She adds that math vocabulary such as evaluate, estimate, difference and factor can be read fluently yet not understood. Her recommendations are to build early decoding, fluency and vocabulary, explicitly teach the common terms in word problems, model the steps aloud, and remind math-minded students that real-life problems come wrapped in language.
points: Memorization, pattern recognition, automaticity and fluency matter for literacy just as they do for numeracy and can be practiced in the same way.
Reading dysfluency overloads working memory, so a student strong in math can still fail a word problem.
Math-specific vocabulary needs explicit teaching because students can pronounce words like factor and difference without grasping their meaning.
Strong reading skills are presented as a precondition for strong problem-solving, even for self-described math-minded students.
quotes: Word problems require students to find solutions by applying their math skills, but first they must apply their literacy skills to understand what problem they have to solve. If they struggle with the latter, it may not matter how strong they are in math.
Parents often assume the problem lies in their children’s math skills and discount the role literacy skills play in solving word problems.
If recognizing words on the page is anything but instant, it will require conscious thought, and that thinking will crowd out more advanced cognitive activities that are required to understand text.
Helping students improve their ability to solve math word problems begins with improving their reading fluency.
When students encounter words like “evaluate,” “estimate,” “difference,” and “factor,” they may not struggle to read them, but they might not be able to make meaning from them.
Parents and teachers can help students better understand math vocabulary by explicitly teaching the common terms used in word problems.
Strong reading skills are a requirement for strong problem-solving skills.
